w: Paris's forgotten railway belt once circled the whole city, then sat abandoned from 1934 until buddleia, foxes and graffiti moved in. A stretch near the Peupliers gate is now open to walk, rails still underfoot and birdsong where trains used to run. The closest thing the city has to wilderness.
s: an abandoned railway belt, reclaimed by weeds and walkers
_facts: 32km circular railway built around Paris between 1852 and 1869
passenger service ended 1934; line fully abandoned by 1993
around 7km of the ~32km total is now open to the public across several arrondissements
overgrown sections host over 200 recorded species of flora and fauna

n: Butte Bergeyre & the Clos des Chaufourniers
w: A hilltop village of roughly a thousand residents, reached only by three staircases or one winding road, hides one of Paris's last vineyards behind an unassuming fence. Clos des Chaufourniers yields barely a hundred litres a year, never sold, while the view over the rooftops runs clean to Sacre-Coeur.
s: a hidden hilltop village with one of paris's last vineyards
_facts: Butte Bergeyre sits on a former quarry hilltop in the 19th arrondissement, elevation about 100m
the Clos des Chaufourniers vineyard was planted in 1995, roughly 600 sq m of Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Muscat, Chasselas and Pinot Noir
the vineyard produces about 100 litres of wine a year and is not sold commercially
the western edge of the Butte gives panoramic views toward Montmartre and Sacre-Coeur

w: Thirty-five houses on a cobbled cul-de-sac, painted pastel pink, sky blue and lime green by residents who wanted their street to feel like somewhere else entirely. It worked almost too well: what was once a quiet secret near Gare de Lyon now needs gates and set visiting hours to keep photographers off the doorsteps.
s: a rainbow cul-de-sac that got too famous for its own good
_facts: 144m pedestrian street in the 12th arrondissement, built 1865-1868
named after lawyer and politician Adolphe Cremieux
35 terraced houses painted in pastel colours by residents
became an Instagram hotspot and now has restricted access hours to manage crowds

w: Behind an unmarked door on Boulevard de Strasbourg, a fourth-generation fan maker still restores and folds by hand in a workshop that doubles as one of Europe's largest fan collections. The showroom is preserved as it was in 1893, tools laid out mid-repair, open only a few afternoons a week.
s: a working fan-maker's atelier turned tiny museum
_facts: private museum run by Anne Hoguet, a fourth-generation fan maker, at 2 Boulevard de Strasbourg
housed in the 1893 Lepault & Deberghe showroom, classified as a historical monument
collection includes over 400 fans on display from a holding of 2,000+ pieces spanning the 18th-20th centuries
open Monday to Wednesday afternoons only

w: Ring the bell at a private mansion near Avenue Foch and a manufacturers' union lets you in to see the fakes: knockoff watches, bootleg trainers, counterfeit perfume, lined up next to the real thing. Founded in 1951 to embarrass forgers into behaving, it remains one of the city's best-kept secrets.
s: ring the bell to see the world's best fakes
_facts: founded 1951 by Unifab (Union des Fabricants) to educate the public on counterfeiting
housed in a private mansion (hotel particulier) at 16 rue de la Faisanderie, 16th arrondissement
collection of several hundred objects across 6 rooms covering 200 sq m
visitors must ring a doorbell to be let in

w: A stone rotunda topped with a lantern-shaped cupola once guarded the head of Belleville's medieval water supply, built around 1600 to watch over the aqueduct that fed the city's fountains. A double staircase still spirals down to the old collecting basin, opened to the public only on Heritage Days.
s: a medieval water-tower rotunda, open one weekend a year
_facts: built between 1583 and 1613 as the main inspection chamber for the Belleville aqueduct
rotunda-shaped structure topped by a cupola, named for the lantern that once sat on top
a double stone staircase inside leads down to the basin that collected the hilltop's water
not normally open to the public; accessible during the Journees du Patrimoine (Heritage Days)

w: A derelict 19th-century train station at Porte de Clignancourt now keeps chickens and beehives along its overgrown tracks, part cafe, part urban farm, part reclaimed slice of the old Petite Ceinture line. Sunday brunch is served with vegetables grown a few metres from the old platform edge.
s: brunch, chickens and beehives on a dead railway platform
_facts: opened 2014 in a 19th-century railway station that closed to trains in 1939
straddles the Petite Ceinture line at 83 Boulevard Ornano, Porte de Clignancourt
runs an urban farm along the old tracks with beehives, chickens, goats and compost from the cafe
built around a 'reduce, reuse, recycle' concept, hosts markets and workshops
